clue.text: Guts involved in manifesto machinations

indicators.note: what is involved in something forms part of it, so the letters sit inside the run of words that follows

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Political scheming over a party manifesto, with guts needed or guts churned.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles the word break: manifeSTO MACHinations.
explanation.definitionFit: Guts can mean the belly or courage, and the word in the grid carries both senses as a noun.

clue.text: A cold aristocrat mounts TV presenter — he'll no doubt make a double entry

definitions.text: he'll no doubt make a double entry

parts.note: taken as written
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap
a count is a nobleman
Ant McPartlin, of the British TV double act Ant and Dec

explanation.surface: A chilly nobleman climbs on top of a television host, who then makes a dramatic double entrance.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'mounts' means sits on top of, so the first three pieces stack above the presenter. Ant is one half of the British presenting duo Ant and Dec.
explanation.definitionFit: Double-entry bookkeeping records every transaction twice, as debit and credit, which is the professional work of someone keeping company books.

parts.note: the eight letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A jab at the US Republican party for cosying up to the far right, with its conservative soul called evil.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the long front half of the clue; only the last four words make letters.

clue.text: Sod all on Unite that's helpful

parts.note: sod all is nothing, which is zero, the letter O
to fuse is to join together

explanation.surface: A grumble that the trade union Unite has done nothing useful.
explanation.walkthrough: Unite is a big British trade union, but here it is just the verb 'unite'. In a down clue 'on' puts the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that serves a purpose or gives practical benefit is described by the phrase, an idiomatic equivalent of that adjective.

clue.text: Newspaper assistant, Cyclops and Reg about to go under

parts.note: a sub-editor checks and trims copy on a paper

indicators.note: 'about' can mean around and in disorder, so the letters are scattered into a new arrangement

parts.note: the setter, Cyclops, refers to himself as me
the name taken as written

explanation.surface: A newspaper sub, the setter and a colleague called Reg are all about to go bust.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's pseudonym stands for ME. 'Go under' looks like business failure, but it is used literally.
explanation.definitionFit: To sink beneath the surface of water is the literal meaning of the phrasal verb, which the word means exactly.

clue.text: PM forced to quit — heaven!

definitions.meaning: a British prime minister who resigned after the 1956 Suez crisis
the garden of paradise in Genesis

explanation.walkthrough: The British prime minister resigned in 1957 in the wake of the Suez fiasco; the same name is the biblical paradise.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical garden is used generally for any blissful place, while the surname belongs to the PM who resigned after Suez.

clue.text: Shady, in the manner of a 19th-century PM

parts.note: Earl Grey, British prime minister 1830 to 1834
the suffix meaning somewhat like

explanation.surface: A sly comparison of some dodgy dealing to a Victorian-era premier.
explanation.walkthrough: The suffix comes from 'in the manner of' and is placed after the name. 'Shady' looks like dishonest but means dim in colour.
explanation.definitionFit: A colour tinged with grey is dull and dim, like something lying in shade, so the adjective fits literally.

clue.text: Parasite journalist Dicky given a bollocking

parts.note: a tick is a blood-sucking parasite
ED is short for editor
dicky means unwell or not right, as is off

explanation.surface: A bloodsucking hack called Dicky gets a severe telling-off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dicky' looks like a name but is British slang for shaky or unwell, as in a dicky heart. A bollocking is a British slang term for a severe scolding.
explanation.definitionFit: To be scolded sharply is the meaning of the phrasal verb in its passive form, matching the rude British slang.

clue.text: Kissinger's other milk producer?

indicators.note: the statesman spoke with a heavy German accent, so his pronunciation of a word is what is wanted

parts.note: said in a thick German accent, the th becomes d

explanation.surface: Henry Kissinger's other dairy line, as if he ran a farm.
explanation.walkthrough: Kissinger famously kept a strong German accent, so 'other' comes out with a d.
explanation.definitionFit: The milk glands of a cow hang in a bag beneath it, which is literally the organ that produces milk.

clue.text: Low church bum

parts.note: to low is to make a cow's sound
CH is the abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: A scruffy idler hanging around a Low Church congregation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Low church' reads as the evangelical wing of Anglicanism, but 'low' is a cow's call. 'Bum' is a verb here, as in bum a cigarette.
explanation.definitionFit: To bum something is to cadge or scrounge it, and the answer is an informal verb meaning the same freeloading.

clue.text: Awful lonesome, with you just starting to head towards bankruptcy?

parts.note: the eight letters to be rearranged

indicators.note: only the beginning of a word is wanted, so just its opening letter is kept

explanation.surface: Someone awfully lonely, with you just starting out, heading for financial ruin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Awful lonesome' reads as American 'awfully lonely', but 'Awful' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A business that keeps making losses is on the road to insolvency, so the verb phrase describes that downhill course.

clue.text: Not an extreme politician, but breaking cistern over Tory's head

parts.note: the seven letters to be rearranged

parts.note: the opening letter

explanation.surface: A moderate politician who nonetheless smashes a toilet cistern over a Conservative's head.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'over' just means the first piece comes before the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A moderate who sits in the political middle ground rather than at either wing is the noun the answer names.

clue.text: Underwear with brief cover — genius!

parts.note: a bra is an undergarment
insurance cover, cut short to its usual abbreviation

explanation.surface: Delight at underwear that barely covers anything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brief' suggests skimpy underwear, but it means abbreviated: cover is insurance, shortened.
explanation.definitionFit: A clever person who does the thinking for a group is called its brains, so the noun stands for a gifted mind.

clue.text: Unhealthy agenda — Labour ends in folly

indicators.note: one thing set in another is placed inside it

parts.note: folly is madness

indicators.note: the ends of words are their final letters, so only those are kept

parts.note: the final letter
the final letter

explanation.surface: A jibe that the Labour party's agenda is sick and ends in foolishness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ends' takes the last letter of both 'agenda' and 'Labour', and the pair goes inside the word for madness just before its final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Dirty, unhygienic conditions are bad for health, so a place lacking sanitation is literally harmful to people's wellbeing.

clue.text: Tiered tax reform? Get rid of foreign element

indicators.note: to reform is to form again, so the letters are reshaped into a new order

parts.note: the nine letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A proposal for a banded tax system, then a call to expel outsiders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tax reform' looks like a policy phrase, but 'reform' is the anagram signal for the two words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Sending an accused person back to another country's courts removes an unwanted outsider, which the cryptic phrase describes.

clue.text: Two unknowns start to evolve in rampant variants — a real hindrance in fighting coronavirus

definitions.text: a real hindrance in fighting coronavirus

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it

the start of a word is its opening, so only its first letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter
the eight letters to be rearranged
x is the algebraic unknown, twice

explanation.surface: Covid variants spreading out of control, and the people who make fighting the virus harder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rampant variants' sounds like epidemiology, but 'rampant' scrambles the second word, and the unknowns plus E slot inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: People who refuse or campaign against vaccines undermine public-health efforts, so they obstruct the campaign against the pandemic.

clue.text: Strangle a regulator

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to choke someone by the throat
second meaning: the valve controlling fuel flow to an engine

explanation.walkthrough: Read together it sounds like murdering an official watchdog; the two halves are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a verb for choking someone and a noun for the valve that controls how much fuel reaches an engine.

clue.text: What Trump was supposed to do over USA, before going to the edge

definitions.text: What Trump was supposed to do over USA

parts.note: the prefix meaning before
a side is an edge

explanation.surface: A dig that Trump, meant to run America, instead took it to the brink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over USA' belongs to the definition: one does this over a country.
explanation.definitionFit: A president is supposed to be in charge of the nation, and to be in charge of something is the verb's meaning.

clue.text: Filthy lucre today is empty — it's not tender

indicators.note: something filthy is in a messy state, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: the five letters to be rearranged

parts.note: the first and last letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Filthy lucre' is a set phrase for money, but 'Filthy' scrambles the next word. 'Tender' looks like legal tender; it means kind.

clue.text: Brenda rejected Act? Hit back!

explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye calls Queen Elizabeth II 'Brenda', and ER is her royal cipher. A turn is a variety performance.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis and other ball games, to send the ball back across to an opponent is a verb meaning to strike it back.

clue.text: Timeserver wanting publicity, volatile noise on right

clue.text: Self-contained beers — they might show weight gain

parts.note: the initial letters of the two halves, as in the property-advert shorthand s/c for a self-contained flat

clue.text: see 27ac.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ropey' suggests shoddy, but it means made of rope: a tethered goat cannot go further. The question mark flags this literal take on the idiom.

clue.text: It's not hotter to get screwed continuously

indicators.note: something screwed is twisted, so these letters are turned into a new order

parts.note: the nine letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A cheeky line suggesting it's no sexier to have sex nonstop.
